description:
Hi, I'm Charyhan from Mary city, a high school student who loves robotics. I built an automatic trash detector that identifies the type of trash and opens the correct lid, and I use AI tools to turn ideas into working prototypes fast.

For this hackathon, we're building the Space Mission Design Game: a browser game where players design a space mission by choosing a rocket, instruments, and power system under real mass, budget, and power limits, then simulate whether it succeeds.
summary:
Marscraft is a free, browser-based Mars exploration and colony-building game that turns the real challenges of living on Mars into hands-on learning. Players drive a rover across an endless isometric Martian landscape and collect resources named after real Mars geology, such as basalt, hematite and water ice. They build habitats, solar power, greenhouses, water and recycling systems, and deploy robots that mine, carry and repair. Along the way they must survive dust storms, night-time power shortages and limited supplies.

Marscraft uses genuine NASA data. Our server fetches the live Earth–Mars distance and signal travel time from NASA/JPL Horizons, so messages to Earth wait for the real communication delay. Facts such as gravity, sunlight and air pressure come from NASA's Mars Fact Sheet, and every discovery explains the real science with its source. Game mechanics are clearly labelled as simulations.

Ten guided missions take players from first landing to a self-sustaining colony. It runs on any phone or computer with no installation, in English, Turkish and Russian. Marscraft makes sustainability, engineering and space science accessible and engaging for students and curious minds of all ages.
details:
What it does and how it works

Marscraft is a Mars exploration and colony-building game that runs in any web browser. Players land on Mars with a rover and one storage building, then grow a settlement that can sustain itself.

The core loop:

1. Explore: tap a deposit and the rover drives across an endless isometric Martian world with seven regions: rocky plains, crater fields, mountains, valleys, ancient river channels, ice-rich ground and dusty plains.

2. Collect: gather resources from 12 kinds of deposits named after real Mars geology, including basalt, olivine, hematite "blueberries", gypsum, clay, buried ice, meteorites and old spacecraft debris.

3. Build: unload at base and construct 23 buildings in three tiers. They range from habitats, solar panels, batteries, greenhouses and water extraction to recycling, research labs, communication dishes and a fission power plant.

4. Automate: build six types of robots (mining, transport, repair, exploration, agricultural and multi-purpose) and upgrade their batteries, motors, cargo, tools, navigation and dust armour.

5. Survive: each sol (Mars day) lasts 3 minutes, with real day and night cycles for solar power. Dust storms cut solar output to 20% and damage rovers left outside, so players must plan energy storage and shelter.

Learning through play:

- Ten guided missions teach one real challenge each, from "First Steps on Mars" through "The Frozen Frontier", "Growing Food" and "Surviving the Storm" to "A Sustainable Future". A secret expedition and a free build mode follow.

- Every new discovery opens a science card that explains the real geology, why scientists study it, and its source.

Real NASA data:

- Our server queries NASA/JPL Horizons for today's real Earth–Mars distance and light travel time, and caches the result hourly.

- The Journey to Mars scene shows the live distance. In-game messages and supplies from Earth wait for the real signal delay.

- Physical facts (gravity, sunlight of 586.2 W/m², air pressure of 6.36 mb, day length) come from the NASA NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet.

- Content is clearly labelled as real science, background or game model, so players know what is fact and what is simulation.

Benefits

- Accessible: free, no installation, runs on phones, tablets, school Chromebooks and desktops.

- Multilingual: English, Turkish and Russian.

- Beginner-friendly: a short tutorial, a next-step guide and a one-minute Demo Mode.

- Private: no account needed. Progress is saved only in the player's own browser.

- Honest science: real data is clearly separated from game simulation.

Intended impact

We want to make Mars exploration, sustainability, engineering and robotics understandable for students and curious people of all ages. Players learn by making decisions instead of reading a textbook. They feel why water, energy, recycling and automation matter, and why communicating with Earth is never instant. The same questions of managing limited resources sustainably also apply on Earth.

Tools and technologies

- Languages: TypeScript, HTML and CSS.

- Frameworks: Next.js 16 and React 19, styled with Tailwind CSS 4.

- Graphics: everything is drawn on HTML Canvas, with no game engine or graphics libraries. The only runtime dependencies are Next.js and React.

- Data: the NASA/JPL Horizons API, called from the server, and the NASA NSSDCA Mars Fact Sheet.

- Hosting and code: deployed on Vercel. Version control with Git and GitHub.

- Testing: Vitest, with 202 automated tests.

- Development help: an AI coding assistant, Claude Code. Every feature was tested.

- Hardware: a laptop. No special hardware is required to play.

Creativity

- Real Mars geology becomes collectable resources, and the real Earth–Mars signal delay becomes a game mechanic.

- Robots act as independent workers that players can inspect and manage.

- The world is endless and procedurally generated, and metal deposits slowly regrow, so exploration always matters.

- Real and simulated content is clearly labelled.

Factors we considered

- Scientific honesty: we only claim what is real, and label simplifications.

- Accessibility: mobile-first controls, three languages, no install and a gentle learning curve.

- Performance: a lightweight build that runs on low-end devices.

- Security: API calls stay on the server, saved games are checked and cleaned when loaded to block tampering, a backup save is kept, and the site sends strict browser security headers.

- Reliability: if NASA's service is unreachable, the game keeps working with a fallback signal delay.

- Scope: a simple architecture that one developer can maintain.
